title: Self-directed vs managed accounts
subtitle: Account types
openingQuestion: You don't have much time to research stocks, want to invest long-term but still control costs. Which option below fits a 'managed account' in the common Vietnamese sense?
openingOptions: Personally placing multiple buy/sell orders yourself throughout the day based on breaking news
Personally opening a securities account at a securities company, personally researching and placing buy/sell orders for individual stocks
Investing in an open-ended fund managed by a fund management company on your behalf
Opening a regular bank account to save money and making no investment at all
explanation: A self-directed account is one where you make all buy/sell decisions yourself and only pay trading fees; a managed account is one where you hand that job to a professional team and pay a management fee based on assets. The choice doesn't depend on how skilled you are but on whether you have the time and discipline to monitor it. One question worth asking upfront: how is the advisor compensated, since that shapes the advice they give.

diagram.label: Self-directed: choose stocks and decide yourself
Managed: hand it to fund experts
A trade-off between control and expertise

realWorldExample.company: Self-directed through SSI/VNDirect vs managed through VinaCapital/Dragon Capital
realWorldExample.description: An investor can open a securities account at SSI or VNDirect, personally research and place buy/sell orders for individual stocks (a self-directed account). Or they can buy open-ended fund certificates like VESAF, VEOF from VinaCapital or DCDS from Dragon Capital through the Fmarket platform - where a professional fund management team decides which stocks to pick and when to trade on the investor's behalf (a managed account), in exchange for charging a management fee of around 1.5-2%/year.

quiz.question: What is the main advantage of a self-directed account compared to a managed account?
options: No trading account of any kind is needed to still be able to invest
Lower cost and full control over decisions
It always delivers higher returns than a managed account
No exposure at all to overall market volatility risk
quiz.explanation: A self-directed account doesn't incur an annual fund management fee (only paying a trading fee each buy/sell), and the investor decides the entire portfolio themselves. The trade-off is having to personally spend time researching and being fully responsible for their own decisions.

quiz.question: Investing through an open-ended fund (a managed account) suits which group of investors best?
options: Someone with plenty of time and knowledge to analyze stocks themselves
Someone who wants to avoid every type of fee in investing entirely
Someone busy, willing to pay a fee to have a management team
Someone who only wants to day-trade repeatedly during the session
quiz.explanation: Open-ended funds suit someone who prioritizes convenience, has no time/knowledge to analyze on their own, and is willing to pay a management fee (usually 1.5-2%/year) in exchange for having their portfolio run by a professional team.

quiz.question: Which management model does a robo-advisor (a feature on some modern investing apps) operate under?
options: Only applies to government-issued bonds
A form not yet recognized under Vietnamese law
Fully self-directed, with no algorithm involvement at all
A managed account, automated by an algorithm
quiz.explanation: A robo-advisor is a form of 'management' but uses an algorithm instead of a human making decisions directly, usually at lower cost than traditional active management thanks to automation, suiting someone who wants management but at a more affordable cost.

quiz.question: An open-ended fund charges a 2%/year management fee while an index ETF charges only 0.2%. What must happen for that fee gap to be worth it?
options: The open-ended fund must consistently outperform the benchmark index by more than 1.8%/year after fees
The open-ended fund just needs to have positive returns in most of its operating years
The open-ended fund must have a larger asset scale than the ETF tracking the same index
No condition is needed, since a higher fee always comes with a more skilled management team, a bar most active funds fail to clear
quiz.explanation: The fee is a certain loss, while the outperformance over the index is uncertain. To be worth paying 2% instead of 0.2%, an active fund must generate sustainable outperformance larger than that fee gap - something most funds worldwide fail to achieve over many years.

quiz.question: What is the biggest conflict of interest to watch out for when a staff advisor recommends an investment product?
options: They usually aren't trained on the very products they're distributing
They may receive different commission levels depending on which product you choose
The law bans them from discussing a product's risk when advising a customer which is the incentive worth questioning directly
They're only permitted to recommend exactly one product per customer
quiz.explanation: When compensation is tied to the product sold, advice may lean toward the product paying the highest commission rather than the product best suited to you. The question worth asking directly: how is the advisor compensated, and do they have a duty to put the client's interest first?

keyTakeaways: Self-directed account: the investor researches and places buy/sell orders themselves, incurring no annual management fee but needing time and knowledge
Managed account (open-ended fund, entrusted investment): a professional team manages the portfolio for you, charging an annual management fee (usually 1.5-2%/year in Vietnam), suiting busy people
A robo-advisor is an intermediate form: automated management by algorithm, usually at lower cost than traditional management
The choice depends on each person's time, knowledge, and willingness to pay a fee - no option is 'always right' for everyone

practicePrompt.question: You work full-time, have no time to research corporate financial statements, but have VND 200 million you want to invest long-term for 10 years. Which option fits your situation?
options: Invest in a professionally run open-ended fund, paying a management fee instead of researching stocks yourself
Open your own securities account and use whatever little time you have left each day to try analyzing and picking individual stocks yourself
Don't invest at all until you have enough free time to thoroughly research the entire stock market on your own
Ask a friend with no financial expertise to place buy/sell orders on your behalf with no formal management agreement at all
practicePrompt.explanation: An open-ended fund suits someone busy, lacking time for in-depth research, willing to pay a management fee to have a professional team manage the portfolio on their behalf.

summary.keyIdea: Self-directed account: the investor researches and places buy/sell orders themselves, incurring no annual management fee but needing time and knowledge
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: Managed account (open-ended fund, entrusted investment): a professional team manages the portfolio for you, charging an annual management fee (usually 1.5-2%/year in Vietnam), suiting busy people

application.title: Calculate the management fee you're paying
application.message: If you currently have money in an open-ended fund, look up the annual management fee stated in the prospectus and ask yourself whether you have enough time and knowledge to self-manage instead of paying that fee.
application.secondary: No option is 'always right' - what matters is knowing what you're paying to get what in return.

sections.text: After deciding to invest in stocks, the next question is: pick stocks and place orders yourself, or let someone else (or an algorithm) do it for you? This is the choice between a self-directed account and a managed account.

With a self-directed account, you open a securities account at a securities company (SSI, VNDirect, VPS, TCBS...), personally research financial statements, personally decide which stocks to buy, when to sell, and take full responsibility for the results. Costs consist only of the trading fee each buy/sell (usually 0.1%-0.25% of trade value) and the 0.1% tax when selling, with no annual management fee.

With a managed account, you hand your investment decisions to a professional third party. The most common form in Vietnam is an open-ended fund (mutual fund): you buy fund certificates from fund management companies like VinaCapital, Dragon Capital, VCBF... through a platform like Fmarket, and the fund management team decides portfolio allocation, stock selection, and trade timing. In exchange, you pay an annual management fee (expense ratio), usually 1.5-2%/year for an active fund in Vietnam.

items: Self-directed account: full control, lower cost, but requires time and knowledge to research yourself
Managed account (open-ended fund): an expert manages on your behalf, convenient, but incurs an annual management fee
Robo-advisor: a 'managed' version by algorithm, usually cheaper than a traditional active fund
You can combine both: self-manage part of your capital (stocks you understand well), and put the rest through an open-ended fund

left.label: Self-directed
left.text: You pick stocks yourself, place orders through a securities company. Suits someone with time, knowledge, and who wants to control every decision. Cost: trading fee + 0.1% tax when selling, no management fee.

right.label: Managed (open-ended fund / entrusted)
right.text: An expert or algorithm manages the portfolio on your behalf. Suits someone busy, lacking deep expertise, prioritizing convenience. Cost: annual management fee (usually 1.5-2%/year for an active fund).

sections.label: No option is 'always better'
sections.text: A self-directed account doesn't automatically deliver a higher return - many self-directed investors lose money from a lack of discipline or knowledge. Conversely, a managed account doesn't guarantee it always beats the market - many active funds have lower net-of-fee performance than even a simple passive ETF. The choice should be based on your own time, knowledge, and willingness to pay a fee, not on a belief that 'either way you win'.

lines: Self-directed gives you control and lower cost, in exchange requiring time and knowledge; managed gives you convenience, in exchange for an annual management fee.
Many investors choose to combine both - you don't have to pick absolutely one direction or the other.
